segments.text: Good morning, and welcome all of you to today's lecture.
This is the first lecture of a series of lectures about the relationship between diet, health, and disease.
What I want to do in this series is to provide evidence which shows that diet,
in addition to supplying material for the growth and maintenance of the body, as well as the necessary energy for it to function,
also contains two groups of substances.
One tends to produce pathological changes and ill health, and the other helps the body to protect itself.
First, let's take a look at the history of the relationship between food and disease.
This was initiated by two discoveries.
One was the work of Eichmann, who proved in 1897 that berry berry was due to the absence from the diet of a substance found in many foods, especially in cereals.
The substance came to be known as anti-berryberry or vitamin B1. The other
was the discovery of Holstenfrolich in 1907 that fresh foods, especially fruits
and vegetables, contained a substance in whose absence from the diet the disease
known as scurvy developed. This substance is now known as the anti-scorbutic
vitamin, or vitamin C. Both these discoveries led to not only the establishment of the etiology
of Berry Berry and scurvy, but also a new angle of thought that dietetic constituents are essential
to the maintenance of health. Indeed, they led to investigations which ultimately made it clear
that many of the commoner diseases of civilized man had a dietetic factor as a basis.
So in order to supply evidence that common foods consumed by mankind include both protective and
harmful elements, I propose to refer to three practical problems. First, the condition of the
bones and teeth. Second, degenerative changes in the central nervous system. And last but not
least the liability of human beings to infection.
Now let's look at our first example of how eating can affect your body, in this case
bones and teeth.
All of you here may know that the most important factor in producing well calcified bones
and teeth is vitamin D. No matter what you eat for your meal, assuming that they are all
natural foods, a sufficiency of vitamin D will ensure perfect calcification of bones and
teeth, even when the amount of calcium and phosphorus intake is surprisingly low.
On the other hand, if vitamin D intake is insufficient and the body is not exposed to
sunlight, however much calcium and phosphorus you consume, your bones and teeth will suffer
decalcification. However, there are occasions when the influence of calcium and phosphorus intake
is of great importance. It's when the amount of vitamin D you take is moderate but insufficient.
The best example for this is seen when the main food carrying vitamin D is butter. In
this circumstance, the addition of calcium salt results in great improvement of bones and teeth.
In short, imagine the relation of calcification to vitamin D, calcium and phosphorus intake
like this. High vitamin D intake plus low calcium and phosphorus intake equals healthy
bones and teeth. With moderate vitamin D intake, the more calcium and phosphorus intake,
better. Very low vitamin D intake plus infinite calcium and phosphorus intake
still equals imperfect calcification of bones and teeth. So far I've only
mentioned those food factors aiding calcification. However, there is one
group of foods that is outstanding because it interferes with the
deposition of calcifying salts in bones and teeth. Those foods are cereals.
There's a wide difference between cereals in this respect.
For instance, as far as animal experiments are concerned, oatmeal is the worst of all
examined, and white flour interferes least with the calcifying process.
The thing is that oatmeal is far richer in calcium and phosphorus than white flour.
This means a greater deficiency of calcium and phosphorus can be brought about by diets
which actually contain more of these substances, so that an analysis of mineral intake may
be quite misleading.
This may well emphasize that the calcifying effect of vitamin D will always antagonize
the anti-calcifying effects of cereals.
You can see that African natives almost always have well-calcified teeth.
They are all white and shiny, and evenly arranged in powerful, well-grown jaws, despite
the fact that their diets are largely composed of cereals. It's because their skin is often
unprotected from the sun's rays, which generates high amount of vitamin D. If a native adopts a
European habit of clothing, especially in childhood, then his bones and teeth may be
as poorly calcified as those of average Europeans. On the other hand, when Europeans provide abundant
and vitamin D in the diets of their children, they will grow up with healthy bones and teeth.
Now we'll look at the relation between tooth decay and diet.
